summary:
SARabande is an open platform that answers one question for every field in a dry, pump-irrigated region: did it get water this season, and when? We processed 36 real NASA–ISRO NISAR L2 GCOV products from four orbits (22 June – 1 November 2026) over the Qarshi Steppe, Uzbekistan, where river water is pumped about 180 m uphill.

It responds to Dancing with the SARs by turning NISAR's HH and HV time series into physical events with transparent rules: an HH jump with under 2 mm of rain in the three days before means irrigation; HV rises as crops grow and falls at harvest. Four orbits combined give a view every 5–7 days, and results are checked against NASA HLS and NASA POWER.

A farmer finds a field by GPS or on the map and gets a plain answer: how many times it was watered, when, how that compares with the neighbours, and what to do next. Water users' associations get a list of places to check first.

It matters because here water is electricity, yet no independent, field-by-field record of who got water exists. The same open code works anywhere NISAR flies.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SARabande answers one question for every field in a dry, pump-irrigated region: did it get water this season, when, and how does that compare with the neighbours? It is built on 36 real NASA–ISRO NISAR L2 GCOV products (HH and HV polarizations) from four orbits over the Qarshi Steppe, Uzbekistan, 22 June – 1 November 2026.

- Simple view (default, for farmers): find your field by GPS, by coordinates pasted from Google Maps, or on a zoomable map with town labels, a north arrow and a scale bar. Every ≈10 ha square is coloured: grey = no watering seen, light blue = watered once, blue = watered 2 or more times. Click a square and get a plain answer ("Yes. Watered 6 times this season."), the last watering date, the next predicted satellite pass, a season timeline, a comparison with the neighbours within 1 km, and "What you can do" (for example: take this record to your water users' association and ask for your turn, or keep it as proof of irrigation). The record downloads as CSV in one click.

- For water users' associations: one click outlines the squares that show no watering although at least half of the squares around them were watered (188 squares this season). These are the places to check first: a missed turn or a blocked canal, or simply a fallow field, a road or a village. The list downloads as CSV.

- Expert mode: map explorer with time-lapse and swipe comparison, field reports with HH/HV series and an event log showing the exact rule each event passed, four-orbit fusion, validation, the full method, a catalogue of all 37 NISAR products found, CSV/JSON exports and sonification of a field.

- English and Uzbek. The whole platform is one HTML file that works offline: no server, no map library.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Search NISAR L2 GCOV granules over the area with asf_search and earthaccess (ASF DAAC): 37 found, 36 dual-polarization products used from tracks D049, D121, A113 and A041.

2. Read only the area of interest from each HDF5 file and average 2 × 2 pixels in linear power (20 m → 40 m).

3. Multi-date (Quegan) speckle filter, then resample to a common WGS84 grid per track (≈36 × 46 m pixels).

4. Convert to decibels and remove a per-date scene offset (within ±0.7 dB on Qarshi).

5. Average 8 × 8 pixels into cells of ≈10.6 ha.

6. Label every pass-to-pass change with physics rules whose thresholds are stored with the data: irrigation = HH rises ≥ 2 dB and ≥ 0.5 dB more than HV, with < 2 mm of rain in the previous 3 days (NASA POWER, based on GPM IMERG); growth = HV rises ≥ 1.5 dB and RVI ≥ 0.05; harvest = HV falls ≥ 2 dB and RVI ≥ 0.05; open water arriving or receding; flooded vegetation; disturbance.

7. Package everything into one HTML file; the browser computes field answers, neighbour comparisons and reports live.

The physics: NISAR's L-band wave is 24 cm long. Water raises the soil's dielectric constant from about 3–5 (dry) to 20–30 (wet), so HH backscatter jumps after irrigation. HV comes from volume scattering in leaves and stems, so it follows growth and harvest.

RESULTS AND VALIDATION

- 2–3% of the land shows a fresh irrigation pulse at each pass in early July, below 1% from September; all four orbits agree independently.

- Four orbits give 19 dates instead of 9: a view every 5–7 days.

- Example field: watered on 6 dates, seen by 4 of 4 orbits. 17% of the area received water at least once.

- Per field, radar HV follows NASA HLS NDVI with a median correlation of 0.66–0.79 on all four tracks, against 0.32–0.60 for a shuffled-field control. Only one day with ≥ 1 mm of rain from June to October.

- The same code maps the Tonle Sap flood pulse in Cambodia: open water ≈1,220 → ≈1,520 km² from July to October.

BENEFITS

- Farmers get independent proof and a comparison with their neighbours, plus a clear next step.

- Water users' associations get a to-do list and can plan fair rotations without field visits.

- Basin authorities see which areas received water at each pass; insurers and lenders can verify irrigation remotely.

- No sensors in the field, free data, a view every 5–7 days, through clouds and at night. Optical satellites could not do this here: for 7 of our 19 radar dates there was no usable optical image within 3 days.

INTENDED IMPACT

In the Qarshi Steppe, river water is pumped about 180 m uphill, so water is electricity. Yet no independent, field-by-field record of who got water exists. A published study (Djumaboev et al., 2019) estimated that optimized irrigation schedules could save 575 million m³ of water and 259 GWh of electricity there. We do not claim that saving; we provide the measurement that managing it requires. Plan: a free pilot season with one water users' association in Qarshi, farmers' irrigation dates as the next validation, then a per-hectare subscription for associations, clusters and insurers (target price about $1 per hectare per season, to be tested), and expansion to other provinces (Uzbekistan has 4.2 million ha equipped for irrigation, FAO AQUASTAT) and to any region NISAR covers.

TOOLS

Python (asf_search, earthaccess, h5py, h5netcdf, fsspec, xarray, rioxarray, rasterio, pyproj, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, Pillow, PyYAML, pytest: 19 tests pass); HTML, CSS and JavaScript without frameworks, Canvas, SVG and the Web Audio API; NASA Earthdata / ASF DAAC; fonts Unbounded, Manrope and JetBrains Mono (SIL OFL). Hardware: one laptop. Open source, Apache-2.0.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- Four NISAR viewing geometries are treated as four independent witnesses: processed separately, then combined. This doubles the revisit rate and gives a built-in consistency check.

- No black box: every detected event shows the physical rule and the numbers it passed.

- A radar time series becomes one plain question, one answer and one next step; the neighbour comparison turns data into evidence for a fair turn of water.

- Sonification lets people hear a field's season, and the whole platform runs offline from a single file, even in a village office without internet.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Users: mentors told us the first version was too complex for farmers, so we made a simple view the default and kept the expert tools one click away; English and Uzbek; mobile and GPS.

- Scientific honesty: the data are provisional; 12-day sampling per track can miss short irrigations; a 10 ha cell can mix two fields; ploughing can mimic wetting (reduced by the HH–HV margin and the four-orbit agreement); HV tracks change, not the NDVI level (pooled r ≈ −0.1). Farmers' own irrigation dates are our next check.

- Cost and access: free NASA data, processing on a laptop (one track-season ≈ 20 MB after processing), one offline file.

- Fairness and privacy: no personal data; flagged squares mean "check first", not "someone did wrong".

- Rules: NASA data at the core, every source referenced, AI assistance declared (Claude, Anthropic, for code and text), no AI-generated images, no NASA branding.
